post_title: How to trace a pattern from a book (or image)
post_details: Hi there! Since college I've been using the Pattern Magic books to help me better understand patterns and try out new shapes. In this tutorial I demonstrate how to scan and create a pattern from a book or image. By working this way, I am more easily able to translate paper patternmaking into 3D. VIDEO: HOW TO TRACE A PATTERN FROM A BOOK STEPS BELOW: Step 1: Scan your pattern, make sure the page is flat and not warped/distorted. Then crop away unnecessary information. Step 2: Create a rectangle in CLO that encompasses the size you need for the pattern (in my case 74 cm). I worked that out by seeing the 66cm measurement on the pattern, and adding additional allowance as a buffer. Step 3: Drag &amp Drop your pattern image onto the rectangle as a Texture. Step 4: Create a reference line (you will be using this as a reference for how large to make the pattern texture). Pick something easy, for example, I used the 66cm Center Back Measurement. Step 5: Scale the Texture to match the image to your reference line. If you already know what size it needs to be, you can simply type it in under Texture Transformation in the Property Editor. Step 6: Use the Internal Polygon/Line Tool to Trace the pattern edges. Tip: once finished, hide the texture on the pattern to make your workspace less chaotic. Step 7: Extract out patterns (2 Steps) a) For FULL SHAPES, use the Transform Pattern Tool to right-click &gt Clone as Pattern b) for OPEN SHAPES / INDIVIDUAL LINES use the Trace Tool to select all relevant pattern edges, right-click &gt Trace as Pattern Step 8: Create your 3D model from your pattern! Good luck!

post_details: Is there a way to optimize or control the polygon count of the Avatar and the Garments before exporting?

comments.comment_body: Hi Jeremy, Garment polygons are controlled by Particle Distance. Instead of polygon count, you're controlling the size of each polygon and the pattern will automatically refill. Select any of the pattern pieces you want, then navigate to the Property Editor on the side to see the Particle Distance number: By default it's 20mm and we recommend changing everything to around 5mm for better quality before exporting, though the lowest number is 0.8mm. Each pattern piece can have a separate Particle Distance, and you can change the values at will. Just remember to Simulate after each change and that lower values will result in slower simulation. If you'd rather have Quads instead of Triangles, the Misc menu in the Property Editor allows you to change the type of mesh and tells you the Face/Vertex counts. The default Avatar's polygons can be subdivided to smooth out its surface. Select it in the 3D Window, then check Divide Mesh in the Property Editor. It's not possible to do more comprehensive editing on the Avatar unless you just want to change the texture maps.

post_details: If the tip of the fabric falls into a diagonal line When the end of the fabric falls into a diagonal line, measure the end nearest to zero. If the fabric is bent inwards If the end of the fabric bends inwards, rotate it back and measure the length when the end of the fabric meets the ground at 90 degrees. If the fabric bends outwards When the fabric bends outwards, measure the Contact Distance where the fabric touches the ground. When measuring Length, measure the same point used to measure the Contact Distance. If the tip of the fabric sticks to the machine and falls off (Solution) Turn the lever to pull out half of the fabric. Turn the lever in the opposite direction to insert the fabric. Continue turning until the end of the fabric meets the ground at 90 degrees. Then, measure the Length.

post_details: There is a change in the method of Stretch Test, so i share it below. When the fabric is pulled by 1mm and the force is less than 0.01kgf 1. Pull the fabric until the force value is 0.01kgf. 2. Starting with the length reached at step 1, check the length and force of each 10mm increment. 3. Record 10 sections. 4. Use a value only when the force difference of each section is at least 0.02kgf. (If the force difference for each interval is less than 0.02kgf, do not use that value.) 5. Finally, select and use values resulted in at least 3 sections and up to 5 sections. (We recommend that you fill out all five sections as much as possible because the more measurements you have, the more accurate the data is.) When the fabric is pulled by 1mm and the force value is over 0.01kgf 1. Check the value of the force when fabric is pulled to 1mm. 2. Starting with the length reached at Step 1, check the length and force of each 1mm increments. 3. At this time, measure 3 to 5 sections. (We recommend that you fill out all five sections as much as possible because the more measurements you have, the more accurate the data is.)

comments.comment_body: Hi Kkuhle! You can save your color palette anywhere in your computer, so don't worry about the file location. To import a palette into CLO, first open CLO and click on Fabric 1 in the Object Browser. Then go down to the Property Editor underneath and click on the Color swatch. In the color window that pops up, click on the little plus sign on the right side (next to Default_Palette) and a browser window will open up to let you open your custom palette. This color window is linked to your entire CLO interface, so you'll only have to load the palette once. You may have to wait a few seconds for the palette to load, depending on how many colors are in it. Note: If your colors are coming in a bit weird, make sure you saved the palette in RGB format or converted it. Since CLO is desktop only, the 3D Window exists in an RGB color space. You can build CMYK colors, but just save a version of your files in RGB and you should be good to go. Anh
